Start here: close an airport → the aircraft held there run late on every later leg → connections break and crews hit their duty limit → an AI dispatcher recommends a fix, with before/after.

Import a flight schedule

Drop a CSV, TSV or JSON file anywhere on this page, choose one, or paste it below. Domino Sky rebuilds each aircraft’s chain of flights, the connecting passengers and the crews, then simulates your day.

  • Needed: origin airport, destination airport, scheduled departure time, scheduled arrival time (any column order; names are matched loosely — e.g. origin/dep/from).
  • Optional: flight number, tail / registration (otherwise rotations are inferred), airline, seats, passengers, and origin_lat origin_lon dest_lat dest_lon for airports Domino Sky does not know.
  • Times: HH:MM, HHMM, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM or ISO 8601. JSON may be an array of flights or {"flights":[…],"airports":[{"code","lat","lon"}]}.

How Domino Sky works

The idea. Each aircraft flies a chain of flights through the day. If a plane is held at one airport, every later flight on its chain starts late — even in cities with clear skies. Late arrivals also break passenger connections and push crews past their legal duty hours.

Try it in four moves

  1. Close an airport — Scenario tab → “Close an airport”: pick the airport, when it closes and for how long (or plant a storm anywhere on the map).
  2. Watch it spread — press Play. The map, the rotation schedule, the flight board and “Where to fix” show which flights are late, why (each delay is traced back along the aircraft’s chain), and how many passengers are stranded. The Crews tab shows duty clocks.
  3. Ask the AI dispatcher — AI Dispatcher tab → “What should I do?”. It recommends an action (swap in a spare aircraft, cancel a rotation, ground-delay program, …) with a before/after table.
  4. Apply it — the day re-simulates and the result is stated again with exact before/after numbers.

Where the numbers come from

All delay, passenger and crew calculations are done by deterministic code (a seeded discrete-event simulation — same inputs, same answer, every time). The dispatcher explains and recommends; it never calculates. Every figure it writes is pulled from the simulator, and a separate audit step then re-reads the finished text and checks each number and clock time against the simulator’s own output; the badge under each message shows the result. With the optional Claude mode, a number the model invents that the simulator did not return is highlighted in red.

Data

The default network is the organisers’ dataset (data/flight_network.json): 16 airports, 70 flights on 16 aircraft, 21 passenger connections with their own minimum connect times, 16 crews with explicit duty windows, 2 spare aircraft and a 30-minute minimum turnaround. With no problem planted, the simulator reproduces its timetable exactly. The India and Worldwide networks are larger synthetic examples on the real map; Import data runs any other schedule (CSV/JSON).
